findings.paper_title: Housing Capital Programme 2026-27: Period 3 Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Twechar Canalside flagship development encounters construction delay, completion pushed to late October 2026
findings.detail: The Council's only active housing construction project has experienced delay during internal fit-out, pushing the anticipated completion from the original programme to late October 2026. This is the flagship project of the Council's new-build programme.
findings.matters: Slippage in the Council's only active construction project indicates execution risk in capital delivery. The project represents part of the £23.9m new-build investment forecast for 2026-27.
findings.figures: £23.9m forecast new-build housing investment across 9 current development sites in 2026-27
findings.quote: The project has encountered some recent delay during the internal fit-out stage and as a result is now anticipated to achieve completion in late October 2026.

findings.paper_title: Housing Capital Programme 2026-27: Period 3 Monitoring Report
findings.headline: New £500,000 Milngavie Police Station acquisition with funding source (borrowing or reprofiling) still undetermined
findings.detail: The Council is acquiring the former Milngavie Police Station (valued at £500,000 by District Valuer) for conversion to up to 10 residential units. The acquisition is subject to Committee approval on 27 August 2026, completion of due diligence by 31 August, and a clawback agreement giving Police Scotland 50% of value uplift if sold within 10 years. Crucially, the funding mechanism—additional Housing Revenue Account borrowing or reprofiling from elsewhere in the capital programme—has not yet been determined.
findings.matters: At a point where the council faces a £4.5m capital underspend, a new £500k acquisition funded through additional borrowing would increase HRA debt servicing costs. The deferral of funding detail until the next report suggests internal constraints on available capital.
findings.figures: £500,000 acquisition cost; up to 10 one and two bedroom flats; 50% clawback if sold within 10 years
findings.quote: The cost of the acquisition of the former Milngavie Police Station will be met through either additional prudential borrowing in the Housing Revenue Account and/or through the reprofiling of other planned expenditure in-year, with details to follow within the next Housing Capital Programme Monitoring Report.

findings.paper_title: Housing Capital Programme 2026-27: Period 3 Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Capital programme variance of £4.5m primarily driven by pause of Campsie View School project pending Community Asset Transfer decision
findings.detail: Forecast expenditure is £37.479m against a budget of £42.889m, a variance of £4.510m (10.5%). This is attributable to the Council's decision to pause the former Campsie View School site at the end of pre-construction pending outcome of a Community Asset Transfer (CAT) application by Lenzie Community Development Trust. The pause delays construction to beyond the current financial year and grant income has been adjusted accordingly.
findings.matters: The £4.5m variance depends on an external decision (CAT approval), creating uncertainty about whether expenditure will accelerate if approved or remain suppressed if rejected. This affects the Council's borrowing requirement and treasury position.
findings.figures: £42.889m approved budget; £37.479m forecast expenditure; £4.510m variance; £5.355m Scottish Government grant funding expected
findings.quote: Council considered the Stage 2 report for the project in June 2026 and have opted to pause the project, pending the outcome of a Community Asset Transfer (CAT) application for the site made by the Lenzie Community Development Trust which remains to be determined.

findings.detail: The partnership required £9.511m in savings for 2025/26. As at Month 12 (Health) and Month 10 (Social Work), only £6.7m had been delivered: £1.9m from Health and £4.8m from Social Work. The savings table indicates a recurring gap of approximately £2.7m.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 14. Financial Performance on Budget 2025 - 2026 Month 12
findings.headline: Pay awards exceeding budget assumptions (4% actual vs 3% budgeted) with future Agenda for Change impact
findings.detail: The council's actual pay award was confirmed at 4% and NHS Agenda for Change staff at 4.25%, against the 3% assumption built into original budgets. Funding has been provided to cover the difference for 2025/26. However, from April 2026 the Agenda for Change working week reduces from 37 to 36 hours, which will require either service reduction or additional staffing investment. NHSGG&C is only providing 75% of the funding requested, with negotiations ongoing.
findings.matters: Workforce cost pressures that exceed budget assumptions, combined with unresolved funding for reduced working hours, signal ongoing staffing-related financial risk for future years.
findings.figures: 4% pay award (vs 3% budgeted), 75% of requested funding for reduced working week
findings.quote: Pay Uplift assumptions of 3% were built into the local authority and NHS budgets for 2025/26. Actual pay uplift for the local authority was confirmed at 4%, and for NHS Agenda for Change staff at 4.25%... NHSGG&C have made available 75% of the funding requested by the HSCP with discussions ongoing between NHSGG&C and SG.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 14. Financial Performance on Budget 2025 - 2026 Month 12
findings.headline: General reserves at only 1.9% of expenditure (well below prudent level), increasing reliance on earmarked reserves
findings.detail: The partnership's general reserves are forecast to be £3.287m as at March 2026, representing only 1.9% of forecast net expenditure excluding set-aside and hosted services. This is below the 2% level recommended in the reserves policy. The partnership is increasingly dependent on earmarked reserves (forecast to be £31.814m) to smooth budget pressures, with limited general contingency.
findings.matters: Low general reserves leave limited headroom for unexpected pressures; a lender would view this as reducing financial flexibility and increasing dependence on earmarked reserves that are often committed to specific initiatives.
findings.figures: £3.287m general reserves (1.9% of net expenditure), £31.814m earmarked reserves
findings.quote: the current forecast underspend of £0.908m will be added during 2025/26 overall increasing the general (contingency) reserves balance to £3.287m as at 31st March 2026 (1.9% of forecast net expenditure excluding set aside and hosted services expenditure).

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 14. Financial Performance on Budget 2025 - 2026 Month 12
findings.headline: GMS contract overspend of £3.1m forecast for 2026/27 would require major funding solution
findings.detail: The GMS (General Medical Services) contract, which has consistently overspent in previous years with deficits increasing year on year, is forecast to overspend by £3.1m in 2026/27. The main cost drivers are superannuation contributions, locum cover, and premises costs. The partnership holds no additional funding to cover this risk.
findings.matters: A £3.1m forecast overspend on a specific contract that has no funding allocation signals a significant budget pressure that will force service reductions or require additional council/NHS funding.
findings.figures: £3.1m potential GMS overspend for 2026/27
findings.quote: Early forecasting for 2026-27 indicates a potential overspend of £3.1m, which would be shared with each HSCP based on their percentage of actual expenditure. The main cost drivers for this are; the cost of Superannuation contributions, Locum cover, and premises cost.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 14. Financial Performance on Budget 2025 - 2026 Month 12
findings.headline: District Nursing re-banding from Band 6 to Band 7 (backdated to May 2022) creates recurring cost pressure
findings.detail: District Nursing job descriptions have been re-evaluated and upbanded from Band 6 to Band 7, with the change backdated to May 2022 for eligible staff. The backdated pay was processed in January-February 2026. This creates a recurring financial pressure for the HSCP going into 2026/27 that was not in the original budget.
findings.matters: A recurring cost pressure from workforce re-banding that was not anticipated when the budget was set reduces financial flexibility and increases future years' costs.
findings.figures: District Nursing Band re-evaluation effective May 2022, processed January/February 2026
findings.quote: The job description for District Nurses has been reviewed and re-evaluated from band 6 to 7 with it being backdated to May 2022 for those eligible, this was paid in January with the backdated element processed in February pay.

findings.paper_title: Item 14. Financial Performance on Budget 2025 - 2026 Month 12
findings.headline: Care at Home service review deferred to 2026/27 due to leadership gap and operational pressures
findings.detail: The Care at Home service review, which was expected to deliver cost reductions, has been deferred from 2025/26 to 2026/27. This is attributed to a leadership gap and operational pressures during the year, meaning planned efficiencies will not materialise this financial year.
findings.matters: Deferred service reviews directly contribute to the unachieved savings gap and signal staffing or capacity constraints that could affect other improvement initiatives.
findings.figures: £687,280 planned savings from Care at Home review not yet delivered
findings.quote: The Care at Home service review was deferred due to leadership gap and operational pressures in year. This will be progressed in 2026/27.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 14. Financial Performance on Budget 2025 - 2026 Month 12
findings.headline: Social work services overspending by £740k on delegated budget, driven by rising demand for care placements
findings.detail: The partnership is projecting a £740k overspend on delegated social work and social care services. This is primarily driven by increased costs for external care at home, residential accommodation, and supported living, reflecting rising demand for care home placements. The current forecast assumes no reduction in waiting lists for residential placements.
findings.matters: Rising demand for care services that cannot be met from budget signals a structural cost pressure that will require either service cuts or additional funding in future years.
findings.figures: £740k overspend on delegated social work budget

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 14. Financial Performance on Budget 2025 - 2026 Month 12
findings.headline: Savings plan delivering only 71% of target with £2.721m shortfall
findings.detail: The partnership planned £9.462m of recurring savings but has achieved only £6.741m to date, leaving a £2.721m gap. The shortfall relates mainly to service reviews that are ongoing and social work services areas where reviews have not yet happened. Some planned savings in Supported Accommodation and Supported Living remain unachieved.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council can hit its efficiency targets; a 28.8% shortfall signals delivery risk on the recurring savings needed to balance future budgets.

findings.quote: of the overall planned savings of £9.462m the HSCP has achieved £6.741m to date, current gap of £2.721m. This gap relates in the main to service reviews that are ongoing and areas within social work services where review has not yet happened

findings.paper_title: 260305 Council Budget Minute FINAL
findings.headline: Unable to recruit to 13 crossing patroller vacancies, with council-wide recruitment difficulties acknowledged
findings.detail: The council acknowledged current country-wide difficulties in recruiting crossing patrollers. There are 13 current vacancies (increased from 12 the previous year despite various advertising methods including social media, leaflets, posters and newspapers). The council declined to allocate additional funding to fill these posts in the 2026/27 budget, citing recruitment difficulties.
findings.matters: Persistent staffing gaps in safety-critical roles indicate either systemic recruitment issues, inadequate pay/conditions, or management challenges; this could signal broader HR or resourcing problems.
findings.figures: 13 crossing patroller vacancies; previously 12 vacancies; country-wide recruitment difficulties
findings.quote: Officers had been unable to recruit to the current thirteen crossing patroller vacancies

findings.paper_title: 260305 Council Budget Minute FINAL
findings.headline: Specific material service reductions approved, including removal of public recycling sites and withdrawal of assisted waste collection provision
findings.detail: The council approved removal of all remaining public (Brings) recycling sites across East Dunbartonshire and withdrawal of free food recycling bags. Assisted waste collection bags will be withdrawn and replaced with increased capacity wheeled bins. These decisions reflect cost-cutting rather than service improvement and may impact service quality perception and resident demand on other services.
findings.matters: Service reductions can create resident backlash, increase demand for complaints/support services, and signal that the council is approaching the limit of what it can deliver; lenders need to assess whether these cuts create liability risk or reputational damage.
findings.figures: Saves cost through removing recycling site operations and bag provision
findings.quote: to remove the remaining public (Brings) recycling sites throughout East Dunbartonshire (PD11). to withdraw the provision of free food recycling bags (PD12).

findings.paper_title: 260305 Council Budget Minute FINAL
findings.headline: Housing Capital Investment Plan approved with £4.858m borrowing in 2026/27 and £46.843m fleet decarbonisation commitment over 10 years
findings.detail: The council approved housing borrowing of approximately £4,858,565 for 2026/27. The Housing Capital Investment Plan includes £9.57m for existing housing refurbishment, £32.419m for affordable housing (308 properties), and £4m for open market purchases. Additionally, the council committed over £46.843m to fleet decarbonisation over the next 10 years. The plan is noted as 'subject to on-going review and revisions to reflect project development, capital pressures, other investment requirements and confirmation of available funding.'
findings.matters: Large capital commitments and borrowing increase debt service costs; a lender needs to verify that the council's debt strategy and cashflow can support these programmes and that capital projects are not at risk of deferral or cancellation.
findings.figures: £4,858,565 housing borrowing in 2026/27; £9.57m existing housing investment; £32.419m affordable housing; £4m open market purchases; £46.843m fleet decarbonisation over 10 years
findings.quote: approved the Housing Capital budget for 2026/27, as detailed in Appendix 2 to the Report, including borrowing of approximately £4,858,565 in 2026/27

findings.headline: Cumulative funding reduction of £162.2m since 2008 with no end in sight to efficiency requirements
findings.detail: The council has faced £162.2m in total funding reductions since 2008. The budget commentary emphasises 'incredibly challenging financial climate' and 'ever-increasing demand for vital services' while costs escalate. The council continues to rely on year-on-year efficiency targets with no indication of stabilisation.
findings.matters: Long-term structural underfunding creates risk that service resilience and asset maintenance will deteriorate; lenders need to assess whether the council's financial position is sustainable or on a declining trajectory.
findings.figures: £162.2m total funding reduction since 2008
findings.quote: He reiterated the amount of money taken from the Council budgets since 2008.

findings.paper_title: 260305 Council Budget Minute FINAL
findings.headline: Revenue budget gap of £23.671m closed by 9.5% Council Tax increase following 13.5% increase the previous year
findings.detail: The council identified a £23.671m financial gap in 2026/27. After applying £18.29m in efficiency savings (management actions and political decisions), a residual gap of £5.38m required a 6.5% Council Tax increase. An additional 3% was added for HSCP, resulting in a total 9.5% Council Tax increase. This follows a 13.5% increase in the previous year, raising concerns about sustainability.
findings.matters: Large and consecutive Council Tax rises signal that efficiency savings are not keeping pace with cost pressures; lenders need to know if the council is reaching the ceiling of what residents will tolerate.
findings.figures: £23.671m financial gap; £18.29m efficiency savings; £5.38m residual gap; 9.5% Council Tax increase (6.5% general fund + 3% HSCP); previous year 13.5% increase
findings.quote: The required expenditure for 2026/27 was £395.641m and indicative income was £371.970m, with a funding gap of £23.671m.

findings.paper_title: 260305 Council Budget Minute FINAL
findings.headline: Health & Social Care Partnership facing critical funding shortfall that requires dedicated 3% Council Tax increase
findings.detail: The HSCP faced a £2.345m funding gap, which the council describes as part of Scotland's Integrated Joint Boards being 'in a critical financial position.' The council committed an additional 3% Council Tax specifically to baseline this HSCP shortfall, on top of the 6.5% required for general fund pressures. The HSCP had a £5.456m loss of funding due to demographic changes, and there are concerns about projected overspend at year-end despite period-10 reporting of £700,000 underspend.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether adult social care demand is manageable and whether the council can sustain funding for vulnerable services; an S151 officer needs to know if social care liabilities are controlled.
findings.figures: £2.345m funding gap; £5.456m loss of funding; 3% Council Tax increase dedicated to HSCP; £700,000 period-10 underspend but projected year-end overspend
findings.quote: Scotland's Integrated Joint Boards were in a critical financial position. It was imperative that the Council support the HSCP and the vital social care services it delivers to the most vulnerable residents.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8g. App7 Finance Risk Register 26-27
findings.headline: Structural demand growth from elderly population (85+ with complex needs) and children with disabilities moving into the area will exceed available budget
findings.detail: Demographics are driving both volume and complexity: 'Increasing elderly population in East Dunbartonshire, particularly for those aged 85+ with a number of co morbidities requiring support' and 'increasing numbers of families with children with disabilities moving into East Dunbartonshire to access school provision who will transition into adult services.' The register notes 'demand for services to meet statutory need exceeds the budget available to deliver.'
findings.matters: Statutory obligations (Adult Support and Protection, Children's Services) cannot be reduced. Structural demand growth that outpaces funding means the deficit will widen each year as the population ages. This is not a cycle the budget can recover from; it compounds.
findings.figures: Current risk score: 4 × 4 = 16 (Priority 2: HIGH). No change in target score (remains 16). Likelihood remains 'Likely'; impact remains 'Major'.
findings.quote: Increasing elderly population in East Dunbartonshire, particularly for those aged 85+ with a number of co morbidities requiring support across a range of health & social care services. Increasing numbers of families with children with disabilities moving into East Dunbartonshire to access school provision who will transition into adult services requiring support to maintain independent living.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8g. App7 Finance Risk Register 26-27
findings.headline: Commissioned care market under severe financial stress from annual pay and contract rate increases with no corresponding funding uplift
findings.detail: Care costs are rising from Scottish living wage increases, national care home contract rate negotiations, and complexity-driven bespoke packages. The HSCP's response is to identify 'savings across service areas or reduction in volume of care packages purchased.' Provider sustainability is explicitly identified as a risk. Current risk score 4 × 3 = 12.
findings.matters: If commissioned providers fail due to unsustainable contracts, the HSCP becomes the provider of last resort. That drives both immediate cost pressure and operational risk, as in-house delivery is more expensive and less flexible.
findings.figures: Current risk score: 4 × 3 = 12 (Priority 2: HIGH). Target score: 3 × 3 = 9 (Priority 3: MEDIUM).
findings.quote: Increase to Scottish living wage (SLW) year on year, increase to national care home contract (NCHC) rates through national negotiation processes, costs pressures for social care providers, local and national re-tendering and contractual arrangements, complexity of care needs resulting in 1:1 / 2:1 care required for bespoke / high cost care packages.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8g. App7 Finance Risk Register 26-27
findings.headline: Unfunded employers' national insurance increase on 6 April 2025, acknowledged as unaffordable by both HSCP and commissioned providers
findings.detail: The NI rate rise was not funded by Scottish Government. The register states: 'In terms of affordability, neither the HSCP or Providers can absorb this unplanned and presently unfunded cost pressure.' Service reductions and contract cessations are expected to offset the cost. This is rated Priority 1 (highest).
findings.matters: An unfunded statutory cost that the organisation has explicitly stated it cannot afford signals immediate budget stress. Commissioned providers are already squeezed by cost-of-living pressures, and the HSCP has decided not to fund them, creating outsourced service risk.
findings.figures: Current risk score: 5 × 4 = 20 (Priority 1: VERY HIGH). Residual likelihood: 5; impact: 4.
findings.quote: In terms of affordability, neither the HSCP or Providers can absorb this unplanned and presently unfunded cost pressure.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8g. App7 Finance Risk Register 26-27
findings.headline: Recurring balanced budget dependent on drawing down reserves, with no sustainable savings plan to replace them
findings.detail: The HSCP is using 'smoothing reserves' to set a balanced budget (FR8, FR9), and multiple risks note reliance on reserves to bridge gaps each year. The register acknowledges that 'reliance on non recurring reserves to set a balanced budget each year is not sustainable and compounds financial pressures into future years' (FR9). With 'significant real terms cuts over the years', identifying new efficiencies has become 'increasingly difficult'.
findings.matters: Persistent reserve drawdowns signal the organisation cannot afford current service levels from recurring funding, and reserves are finite. If external partners stop matching budget gaps or Scottish Government funding deteriorates further, the council faces forced service reductions or insolvency risk.
findings.figures: Current risk score for inability to achieve recurring balance: 5 × 5 = 25 (Priority 1: VERY HIGH). Target score: 4 × 4 = 16 (Priority 2: HIGH), unchanged in likelihood.
findings.quote: Reliance on non recurring reserves to set a balanced budget each year is not sustainable and compounds financial pressures into future years.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8. Financial Planning and Budget Setting 2026-27
findings.headline: Superannuation contribution jump from 6.5% to 17.5% (11 percentage point increase) requires £2.158m baseline adjustment from the Council.
findings.detail: Strathclyde Pension Group implemented a three-year contribution schedule: 6.5% for 2024-25 and 2025-26, jumping to 17.5% for 2026-27. The HSCP baseline had been reduced to reflect the temporary lower rate, so the 11 percentage point increase creates a £2.158m pressure. Ongoing discussions between HSCP and the Council resulted in agreement to increase the baseline funding to match, but SPG is already signalling a further increase to 15% from April 2027 onwards.
findings.matters: The multi-step increase in pension contributions is structural and will persist. The 15% signal for 2027 suggests further pressure ahead. This is a fixed cost that cannot be absorbed through efficiency.
findings.figures: 2024-25 and 2025-26: 6.5%; 2026-27: 17.5% (11pp increase = £2.158m pressure); future planning assumption 15% from April 2027
findings.quote: Strathclyde Pension Group (SPG) implemented a three year package of rates in 2024/25 in relation to employer's superannuation contributions comprising 6.5% for 2024/25, 6.5% for 2025/26 and 17.5% for 2026/27... SPG indicate 15% employer's contribution from 1st April 2027 would be a reasonable future planning assumption.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8. Financial Planning and Budget Setting 2026-27
findings.headline: Pay uplift funding shortfall of £1.402m: local authority received no designated funding for pay awards despite 3.5% uplift assumption.
findings.detail: The budget assumes pay uplifts of 3.5% for social work staff but 'No designated funding was provided for the local authority pay award which creates a pressure of £1.402m' (paragraph 3.50). This pressure must be absorbed within the budget. The NHS received dedicated pay uplift funding, but the local authority share of the partnership's pay costs does not.
findings.matters: An unfunded pay pressure of £1.4m reduces the real scope for service delivery or savings elsewhere. If pay costs exceed the 3.5% assumption or if further pay awards are awarded mid-year, the gap widens.
findings.figures: £1.402m unfunded local authority pay uplift; 3.5% uplift rate assumed for social work, 3.75% for NHS delegated services
findings.quote: Pay Uplift – No designated funding was provided for the local authority pay award which creates a pressure of £1.402m.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8. Financial Planning and Budget Setting 2026-27
findings.headline: Prescribing identified as the single biggest financial risk, with £2.774m earmarked reserve balance being held to cover overspends on a £1.342m stretch savings target.
findings.detail: Prescribing costs are identified as 'singularly the most significant risk to the Partnership in terms of cost and demand volatility' with particular concern about supply chain volatility for medicines on short supply. The partnership is holding a £2.774m prescribing reserve to cover the risk of not achieving a £1.342m savings target (described as a 'stretch target'). The forecast assumes 1.5% volume growth and accounts for global supply chain pressures, manufacturing capacity limits and staffing shortages.
findings.matters: Prescribing is volatile, large (£0.889m pressure noted in budget), and the partnership is already planning to use reserves to cover shortfalls. Any supply chain disruption or volume surge could deplete this reserve and create an in-year deficit.
findings.figures: Prescribing reserve £2.774m; savings target £1.342m (described as stretch); volume growth assumption 1.5%; price fluctuations cited (peak £11.52/item Sept 2025, average £11.29 YTD vs £11.63 prior year)
findings.quote: Prescribing is singularly the most significant risk to the Partnership in terms of cost and demand volatility... There remains an earmarked reserves balance to mitigate the risks of overspending related to prescribing up to £2.774m.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8. Financial Planning and Budget Setting 2026-27
findings.headline: Chief Social Work Officer warns that thresholds for access to services will need to increase and non-essential support will decrease to protect statutory obligations.
findings.detail: The CSWO's statutory advice (section 5.2) states that 'Thresholds for access to services will require to be reviewed and potentially increased, and reduced service delivery in some areas inevitable' and that 'the level of non-essential support that is able to be offered will need to decrease to ensure sufficient resource is available to focus on meeting the needs of the most vulnerable.' The CSWO confirms 'a financial gap remains both for the coming year and into the foreseeable future' and that 'changes are going to be required in how social work services are delivered.'
findings.matters: The statutory social work officer is signalling service reductions and access restrictions as inevitable, not contingent. This is formal notification that current service levels cannot be sustained and that rationing or service cuts are coming.
findings.figures: None quantified in CSWO statement
findings.quote: Thresholds for access to services will require to be reviewed and potentially increased, and reduced service delivery in some areas inevitable. It is also likely that the level of non-essential support that is able to be offered will need to decrease

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8. Financial Planning and Budget Setting 2026-27
findings.headline: Service capacity constraints already in place: waiting lists for Free Personal and Nursing Care despite growing demand from demographic pressures.
findings.detail: The paper reports waiting lists have been introduced 'most notably for access to Free Personal and Nursing Care Funding' to manage demand within tightening resources (paragraph 3.17). Simultaneously, East Dunbartonshire faces the 11th highest projected growth in 85+ population in Scotland (128% growth 2022-2047), yet 'there is no increased budget provision for demographic growth across any service in East Dunbartonshire Council' (paragraph 3.20). Between 2022-2032, the 65+ population is projected to grow 21% and 85+ by 38%.
findings.matters: Growing waiting lists for essential services combined with unprecedented demographic pressure for older adult care signals the partnership is rationing access despite rising need. This creates liability risk and service failure exposure.
findings.figures: 21% growth in 65+ population 2022-2032; 38% growth in 85+ cohort; 128% growth in 85+ population by 2047 (11th highest in Scotland); no budget increase for demographic growth
findings.quote: Where necessary, demand fluctuations in the context of tightening resources have resulted in waiting lists being put in place for some services (most notably for access to Free Personal and Nursing Care Funding).

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8. Financial Planning and Budget Setting 2026-27
findings.headline: Medium-term savings requirement more than doubled: £46-89m over five years (previously £17-38m), with most likely scenario of £48.2m gap.
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy was revised in light of 2026-27 settlement realities. The prior estimate of £17.2m to £38.4m cumulative savings needed through 2025-30 has been raised to £46.0m to £88.9m, with the central scenario now £48.2m. The IJB expects to need £7.6m to £12.7m annually from 2024-25 onwards, peaking at £12.7m in 2025-26.
findings.matters: A near-trebling of the medium-term savings requirement suggests either prior estimates were unreliable or the baseline has fundamentally shifted. This signals sustained, severe financial pressure that cannot be managed through efficiency alone.
findings.figures: Previous estimate £17.2m–£38.4m over five years; revised to £46.0m–£88.9m; most likely scenario £48.2m; annual requirement £7.6m–£12.7m (peak £12.7m in 2025-26)
findings.quote: This will require the identification of £46.0m to £88.9m of savings (previously £17.2m to £38.4m) with the most likely scenario being a financial gap of £48.2m over the next five years.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8. Financial Planning and Budget Setting 2026-27
findings.headline: A £2.9m reserves draw planned for 2026-27 to achieve budget balance, with general reserves falling below prudent minimums.
findings.detail: The IJB faces a £8.192m financial challenge but has identified only £5.287m in savings. This requires a £2.905m draw from earmarked reserves to set a balanced budget. The Chief Finance Officer's report states that general reserves are projected to fall below the 2% prudent level (approximately £4.9m for the partnership). By month 10 forecasting, general reserves were projected at £2.381m.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance a budget indicates structural deficit, not temporary pressure. Falling below prudent minimums removes contingency for unexpected events and signals the partnership is consuming capital to fund operations.
findings.figures: £2.905m earmarked reserves draw; general reserves projected £2.381m against 2% prudent minimum of ~£4.9m; total financial challenge £8.192m
findings.quote: In order to be able to set a balanced budget for 2026/27, the IJB will require to use smoothing reserve totalling £2.905m.

findings.committee: Health and Social Care Partnership Integration Joint Board
findings.paper_title: Item 8. Financial Planning and Budget Setting 2026-27
findings.headline: Social care funding cut by £5.5m due to Scottish Government methodology change, forcing a structural reallocation across care types.
findings.detail: The Scottish Government's review of social care allocation methodology resulted in a £5.456m net reduction to East Dunbartonshire Council's adult social care funding. This split as residential accommodation down 34% (£4.017m reduction), personal and nursing care down 54% (£3.293m reduction), and home-based provision up 17% (£1.854m increase). The IJB received floor mechanism protection of £2.711m, leaving £2.745m of the cut to be managed.
findings.matters: A sudden 34-54% cut to major care service categories threatens service continuity and provider stability, and represents a loss of funding that must be offset by service reductions or cost-shifting.
findings.figures: £5.456m net reduction; residential down £4.017m (34%), personal and nursing care down £3.293m (54%); floor mechanism protection £2.711m
findings.quote: EDC's funding allocations for these services fell by £5.456m. Split between residential accommodation (- £4.017m, which represents a year on year reduction of 34%), personal and nursing care (-£3.293m, a 54% year on year reduction)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - SPPF Report - Budget Reduction Proposals & Residual Gap
findings.headline: Twelve-year pattern of sustained funding cuts with no resolution in sight
findings.detail: The hierarchical budget reduction approach has been operational since 2014. The Council states it has faced "sustained and significant reductions in funding, compounded by increasing costs and demands on services". Efficiency targets continue in 2027/28 (£12.868m) and 2028/29 (£13.265m), indicating no prospect of budget stabilisation.
findings.matters: Demonstrates this is structural, not cyclical. The Council has progressively exhausted lower-cost efficiency options and is now moving to the final tier of its approach: service reduction and cessation. This indicates deteriorating financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Hierarchical approach continuous since 2014; efficiency requirements 2026/27 £18.291m, 2027/28 £12.869m, 2028/29 £13.266m
findings.quote: Having faced sustained and significant reductions in funding, compounded by increasing costs and demands on services, it has become increasingly difficult to avoid service reduction, enforced job reduction or service cessation options.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - SPPF Report - Budget Reduction Proposals & Residual Gap
findings.headline: Significant proportion of stated savings are one-off technical adjustments, not sustainable operational efficiency
findings.detail: Of the £17.236m in management actions, major items are non-recurring or technical accounting moves: MA5 (capital grant application against loans fund £5.975m - one-off), MA7 (income redetermination £1.389m), MA13 (HSCP indicator adjustments £2.949m). These total ~£10.3m of the £17.2m, meaning true operational savings are substantially smaller.
findings.matters: If a significant portion of 'savings' are one-offs or accounting adjustments rather than structural operational improvements, the underlying structural deficit is larger than headline figures suggest and the gap will widen in following years.
findings.quote: Application of Capital Grant against Loans Fund Principal Repayment

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - SPPF Report - Budget Reduction Proposals & Residual Gap
findings.headline: HSCP partner in critical financial position creating joint exposure
findings.detail: The document references Audit Scotland's finding that Scotland's Integration Joint Boards are in "critical financial position" despite real-terms funding increases. A £2.345m HSCP baseline adjustment is baselined in the budget as a prior-year one-off decision.
findings.matters: If the health partnership is in critical position, there are risks to service delivery, potential calls on council reserves to support the partnership, and joint financial exposure through the integrated arrangement.
findings.figures: HSCP baseline realignment £2,345,000; HSCP Council Tax uplift proposed 3%
findings.quote: Despite a real-terms increase in funding, Scotland's Integration Joint Boards (IJBs) are in a critical financial position

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - SPPF Report - Budget Reduction Proposals & Residual Gap
findings.headline: Workforce efficiencies escalating significantly with service reviews commencing in 2026
findings.detail: The Council is targeting employee cost reductions growing from £562k in 2026/27 to £1.124m by 2028/29. Significant service review processes across all services will commence in 2026, and the document acknowledges proposals "will impact on our employees and the working environment", suggesting enforced job reductions are becoming unavoidable.
findings.matters: Indicates structural workforce reductions with associated risks to service continuity and potential unfunded severance costs. Also shows increasing financial pressure forcing moves away from voluntary change toward enforced reductions.
findings.quote: it has become increasingly difficult to avoid service reduction, enforced job reduction or service cessation options

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - SPPF Report - Budget Reduction Proposals & Residual Gap
findings.headline: Residual £5.38m budget gap forces 9.5% council tax increase after £18.3m in savings
findings.detail: After identifying £18.291m in management actions and operational efficiencies, the Council faces a residual gap of £5.380m that cannot be closed through operational means alone. The proposed solution is a 6.5% Council Tax increase for general services and an additional 3% for the Health & Social Care Partnership, totalling 9.5% overall council tax increase.
findings.matters: Shows the council has exhausted operational efficiencies and must rely on significant council tax increases to balance the budget. This signals structural deficit and has practical limits given council tax caps and voter resistance.
findings.figures: Residual Council Gap £5,380,387; Council Tax increase 6.5% general + 3% HSCP = 9.5% total
findings.quote: the residual gap be met from Council Tax, a balanced budget can be achieved

findings.paper_title: East Dunbartonshire Forward in Partnership - General Fund Revenue 202627 and 10 Year Capital Plan
findings.headline: HSCP (Health & Social Care Partnership) faces £2.345m additional pressure in 2026/27 with sector-wide social care overspends of £49m across Scotland
findings.detail: The council has identified £2.345m of HSCP pressures that must be met from Council Tax or further unspecified political options. The Accounts Commission bulletin notes that 15 out of 30 Scottish councils reported social care overspends totalling around £49 million in 2024/25, indicating structural underfunding of social care across the sector.
findings.matters: Social care is a statutory service that councils cannot reduce below legal minimums, making HSCP pressures a structural budget problem rather than discretionary spending that can be cut, and a £2.345m pressure unresolved in the budget setting shows ongoing unmatched demand.
findings.figures: £2.345m HSCP pressure for 2026/27; sector total of £49m social care overspend across 15 councils in 2024/25
findings.quote: with HSCP pressures totalling a further £2.345m to be met from Council Tax or further political options to be determined and agreed at the Budget. 15 out of 30 councils reported overspending on social care services, totalling around £49 million.

findings.paper_title: East Dunbartonshire Forward in Partnership - General Fund Revenue 202627 and 10 Year Capital Plan
findings.headline: Homelessness prevention budget cut by £60,000 and multiple support service reductions proposed alongside school meal price increases
findings.detail: Specific savings proposals include a £60,000 reduction to the homelessness and prevention budget (stated as "deemed achievable in the current position"), removal of AccessAble funding (£9,096), reduction of Snack and Play provision, withdrawal of public recycling sites, withdrawal of free food recycling bags, and ending assisted waste collection for vulnerable users. School meal prices increase 5-6%.
findings.matters: Reductions to services supporting vulnerable groups (homelessness prevention, accessible transport, support services for users needing assistance) during a period of rising demand and HSCP pressures suggests the council is cutting services to populations most likely to create emergency demand elsewhere.
findings.figures: £60,000 homelessness budget reduction; £9,096 AccessAble funding removal; 5% primary school meal price increase; 6% secondary school meal price increase; 4% temporary accommodation rent increase
findings.quote: to a reduction in the Homelessness and Prevention Budget by £60,000 which is deemed achievable in the current position (PD4). o to Increase rent in temporary accommodation by 4% (PD5). o Remove AccessAble funding of £9,096 (PD6).

findings.paper_title: East Dunbartonshire Forward in Partnership - General Fund Revenue 202627 and 10 Year Capital Plan
findings.headline: Sector-wide debt has reached £21.9 billion with 13.5% annual increase, while usable reserves decreased 7% and 16 councils drew on reserves unplanned
findings.detail: The Accounts Commission bulletin referenced in the budget shows Scottish councils collectively increased net debt by 13.5% to £21.9 billion in 2024/25, while usable reserves fell 7%. Sixteen of 30 councils made unplanned use of reserves. The bulletin also notes that 12 councils overspent against General Fund budgets and 15 councils overspent on social care services, totalling £49m.
findings.matters: Sector-wide debt growth and reserve depletion indicate the council is not alone but sits within a broadly deteriorating financial sustainability picture across Scottish local government, suggesting systemic rather than isolated pressures.
findings.figures: £21.9bn net debt sector-wide (13.5% increase); 7% decrease in usable reserves; 16 of 30 councils made unplanned reserve use; 12 councils overspent General Fund; 15 councils overspent social care by £49m total; councils achieved only 89.9% of savings targets with only 31% recurring
findings.quote: Councils' net debt reached £21.9 billion in 2024/25, a 13.5% increase since 2023/24. Usable reserves decreased by 7% between 2023/24 and 2024/25. 16 out of 30 councils made unplanned use of reserves in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: East Dunbartonshire Forward in Partnership - General Fund Revenue 202627 and 10 Year Capital Plan
findings.headline: Large capital programme funded by borrowing will increase debt charges, with £46.843m committed to fleet decarbonisation alone
findings.detail: The council is committing over £46.843m over 10 years to decarbonisation of the fleet, plus substantial spending on new facilities (sports pavilions £1m, new depot £1m, new primary school £3m, accommodation strategy £5m, City Deal £9.1m). All capital spending assumptions are embedded in debt charge budgeting, creating future revenue pressures.
findings.matters: Large capital programmes funded by borrowing increase future debt service costs in a context where the council is already struggling to balance current-year revenue budgets, reducing financial flexibility for future years.
findings.figures: £46.843m for fleet decarbonisation; £1m sports pavilions and pitch upgrades; £1m depot pre-construction; £5m accommodation strategy; £3m Westerton Primary School pre-construction; £9.1m City Deal
findings.quote: A commitment to allocate over £46.843m throughout the lifetime of the plan to 2035/36 to support decarbonisation of the Council's fleet

findings.paper_title: East Dunbartonshire Forward in Partnership - General Fund Revenue 202627 and 10 Year Capital Plan
findings.headline: Section 95 Officer prohibits use of reserves to cover the budget shortfall, citing financial sustainability concerns
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer has given direction that the budget cannot be set with reference to reserves underwriting the gap, and that the council must agree provisions to increase internal financial capacity as a recovery plan. This is stated to be given "in the strongest terms and with reference to the impact of past, present and anticipated future financial challenges."
findings.matters: Reserve restrictions at this level indicate limited reserves available or structural depletion concerns, suggesting the council cannot absorb unexpected pressures or have a genuine safety buffer.
findings.figures: The budget includes direction that reserves cannot underwrite any element of the £23.671m gap
findings.quote: Council should note that the above guidance and advice is provided by the Section 95 Officer to safeguard the immediate financial sustainability of the Council, with no recourse to the planned used of Reserves in 2026/27. This advice is given in the strongest terms and with reference to the impact of past, present and anticipated future financial challenges.

findings.paper_title: East Dunbartonshire Forward in Partnership - General Fund Revenue 202627 and 10 Year Capital Plan
findings.headline: Council requires 9.5% Council Tax increase to set a balanced budget after identifying £23.671m financial gap
findings.detail: The council faces a residual financial gap of £7.725m after management efficiencies (£17.236m) and savings proposals (£1.054m), leaving a shortfall that requires Council Tax to increase by 9.5%. This includes a 3% allocation to Health & Social Care Partnership pressures. The Section 95 Officer (Chief Finance Officer) has directed that reserves cannot be used to underwrite the gap.
findings.matters: A 9.5% Council Tax rise is substantially higher than typical annual increases and signals stress on the council's base funding model and its ability to balance budgets through service efficiency alone.
findings.figures: £23.671m financial gap; £7.725m residual gap requiring Council Tax increase; 9.5% Council Tax increase; £2.345m HSCP pressures within the increase
findings.quote: Managing the financial gap remains a key aspect of the Budget with the previous Appendix (3) reducing the total pressures on the Council from £23.671m to £5.380m, with HSCP pressures totalling a further £2.345m to be met from Council Tax or further political options to be determined and agreed at the Budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2a - SPPF Report - Audit Scotland Supplement to Fin Bulletin
findings.headline: Baselined spending now totals £1.9 billion and restricts councils' spending flexibility on local priorities
findings.detail: The Scottish Government has incorporated £1.9 billion of previously ring-fenced grants into the General Revenue Grant, with £0.8 billion baselined in 2026/27 alone (including £244m for teachers, £257m for health and social care). Although councils nominally have more flexibility, they are still required to spend these amounts on national priorities.
findings.matters: Baselined spend reduces councils' practical flexibility to rebalance budgets locally. This constrains their ability to respond to local pressures and means the identified budget gaps may not be manageable through reallocation.
findings.figures: £1.9 billion total baselined funding; £0.8 billion baselined in 2026/27; £244 million teachers pay; £257 million health and social care
findings.quote: Councils do, however, still need to direct spending to national policies and fulfil their statutory duties.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2a - SPPF Report - Audit Scotland Supplement to Fin Bulletin
findings.headline: Councils increasingly relying on borrowing to deliver capital programmes as Scottish Government funding remains constrained and is set to fall further
findings.detail: Councils have increased borrowing to maintain capital programmes as grant funding declined. With capital allocations now set to reduce further, borrowing will need to increase, raising overall debt levels at a time when funding to service debt is tightening.
findings.matters: Increasing debt combined with declining funding creates a debt sustainability risk. A lender needs to understand councils' borrowing trajectory and whether debt can be serviced from constrained revenue budgets.
findings.figures: Not specified in document
findings.quote: They have increasingly relied on borrowing as Scottish Government funding remained constrained, and now this funding will reduce.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2a - SPPF Report - Audit Scotland Supplement to Fin Bulletin
findings.headline: Councils already deploying reserves and non-recurring savings to manage budget pressures
findings.detail: The Audit Scotland bulletin notes that councils are already drawing on reserves and using one-off savings measures to stay balanced. This unsustainable position indicates financial stress and limited headroom for new pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion is a critical early warning signal for lenders. Once reserves are exhausted, councils have no buffer and must immediately cut services or increase borrowing.
findings.figures: Not specified in document
findings.quote: The cost of delivering services continues to rise, and reserves and non-recurring savings are already being deployed, but significant budget gaps remain to be addressed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2a - SPPF Report - Audit Scotland Supplement to Fin Bulletin
findings.headline: Budget gaps of £997 million cumulatively to 2027/28 significantly exceed the funding increase on offer
findings.detail: Councils identified a £647 million budget gap when setting 2025/26 budgets, with projected cumulative gaps to 2027/28 of £997 million. This structural gap far exceeds the 2% funding increase, indicating councils cannot balance budgets through growth alone.
findings.matters: Identified gaps this size indicate savings plans are falling short and councils are entering a period of service cuts or reserve depletion, both of which affect financial stability and debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: £647 million 2025/26 budget gap; £997 million cumulative gap to 2027/28
findings.quote: Councils identified a budget gap of £647 million at the time of setting their 2025/26 budgets, with a projected cumulative budget gap to 2027/28 of £997 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2a - SPPF Report - Audit Scotland Supplement to Fin Bulletin
findings.headline: Capital funding falling 14% in real terms in 2026/27, with 55% cumulative reduction since 2019/20
findings.detail: Capital allocations are declining in both cash and real terms, with 2026/27 capital funding of £681.4 million representing a 14% annual real-terms reduction from 2025/26. Over six years, capital funding has fallen 55% in real terms, with all but three councils experiencing reductions.
findings.matters: Sustained capital cuts constrain councils' ability to maintain and upgrade infrastructure, forcing increased reliance on borrowing to maintain programmes, which raises debt and financial risk.
findings.figures: £681.4 million capital funding 2026/27; 14% annual real-terms reduction; £769 million (55%) cumulative real-terms reduction since 2019/20
findings.quote: Capital allocations, however, are to decrease in both cash and real terms between 2025/26 and 2026/27, with 2026/27 capital funding of £681.4 million representing a 14 per cent annual real-terms reduction from initial 2025/26 funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2a - SPPF Report - Audit Scotland Supplement to Fin Bulletin
findings.headline: Funding to councils projected to fall in real terms from 2028/29 despite 2026/27 increase
findings.detail: While councils receive a 2% real-terms increase in 2026/27, the Scottish Spending Review projects overall budget reductions of 3.8% in real terms from 2026/27 to 2028/29, with both revenue and capital declining. This creates a medium-term funding squeeze that will intensify financial sustainability pressures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the funding increase in 2026/27 is temporary and that councils face declining real resources, raising questions about debt repayment capacity and service sustainability beyond 2027.
findings.figures: 2% real-terms increase 2025/26 to 2026/27; -3.8% real-terms reduction 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.quote: funding from the Scottish Government to 2028/29 is projected to fall in real terms, challenging councils to consider and implement the measures necessary to ensure the ongoing delivery of services.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27 Including Rent Setting
findings.headline: Nine major affordable housing development sites totalling £32.4m are at varied RIBA stages; one site's timeline is at risk pending a Community Asset Transfer decision.
findings.detail: The council is delivering an ambitious 9-site new-build programme costing £32.419m for affordable housing (section 7.22). Individual sites range from RIBA Stage 2 (Glasgow Road, Kirkintilloch—54 units) to Stage 4 (multiple sites). Most are budgeted to begin construction in 2026-27 or 2027 and complete between 2026 and 2029. The Former Campsie View School site (27 units) is explicitly noted to be subject to a pending Community Asset Transfer application that 'is likely to have an impact on the timescales noted above' and will affect 'the Council's decision as to whether to proceed into the construction phase' (section 7.35-7.36).
findings.matters: A major capital programme with multiple external dependencies (planning, Community Asset Transfer, construction tender, detailed design at varied stages) introduces execution risk. Cost inflation, planning delays, or Community Asset Transfer complications could slow delivery, delay income, and stretch cash flow. Any slippage carries forward borrowing requirements.
findings.figures: £32.419m affordable housing supply capital; 9 sites; 275+ total units; 27-unit site (Former Campsie View) at risk of timing impact
findings.quote: It should be noted that the site is currently subject to an application by a local community group for a Community Asset Transfer and that application is being progressed in parallel with the design process. This is likely to have an impact on the timescales noted above, specifically in relation to the submission of the Stage 2 report and the Council's decision as to whether to proceed into the construction phase of the project, dependent on the status of the Community Asset Transfer application at that point (i.e. June 2026).

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27 Including Rent Setting
findings.headline: Implementation of full-decoration void standard from April 2026 increases cost per property by £1,500 on average and extends void turnaround by over 2 days.
findings.detail: Moving from partial to full decoration of void properties will cost an additional £1,500 per property on average and add just over 2 days to the void turnaround process. The council conducted a review during 2025 and concluded the impact on property appearance and tenant quality justifies the cost increase. This is now embedded in the 2026/27 HRA budget and the 35-year Housing Business Plan.
findings.matters: This is a material cost shift in void management that extends voids and increases annual running costs. If the council experiences unexpected voids (evictions, departures), the cost of managing them has risen. This affects the cash flow and efficiency metrics a lender would monitor.
findings.figures: £1,500 additional cost per void property on average; 2+ days additional turnaround time
findings.quote: whilst the cost per property increases by £1,500 on average, in addition to adding just over 2 additional days to the void turnaround process, the impact on look and feel of the property and the benefit to the new tenant in terms of the quality of the property being presented to them is significant enough to warrant this change in the letting standard at this time.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27 Including Rent Setting
findings.headline: Capital Fund from Revenue (CFCR) of £0.983m is being diverted to reserves rather than funding capital, to support investment in future years.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget generates a CFCR of £0.983m, but this 'will not be applied in 2026/27 and will instead be added to reserves to support investment in future years.' This is a deliberate choice to build the reserve buffer rather than deploy revenue to reduce borrowing need in the current year.
findings.matters: The council is managing cash flow by front-loading borrowing rather than using available revenue savings to reduce debt. If the HRA starts to underperform (lower rents, higher arrears), that CFCR assumption could evaporate, leaving the council unable to fund future investment.
findings.figures: CFCR £0.983m; not applied in 2026/27 but added to reserves
findings.quote: the proposed rent increase of 4% and increased debt charges, noted above, allows for a CFCR of £0.983m however this will not be applied in 2026/27 and will instead be added to reserves to support investment in future years.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27 Including Rent Setting
findings.headline: The council will borrow £4.86m in 2026-27 and cap debt-to-rent below 60% annually, a prudential measure for a major development programme.
findings.detail: Borrowing of £4,858,565 is approved for 2026/27 to fund the housing capital programme. The 35-year Business Plan now caps the debt-to-rent position below 60% in any given year. Where the HRA generates a surplus, it can offset borrowing requirement. The council describes this as 'a prudent approach and demonstrates fiscal responsibility.' This borrowing sits within the revised Housing Business Plan and will be incorporated into the Treasury Management Strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the borrowing trajectory and the council's own debt ceiling. The 60% cap is self-imposed and reasonable, but if rent collection deteriorates or rent growth doesn't materialise, this borrowing becomes less serviceable relative to rental income.
findings.figures: £4,858,565 borrowing 2026/27; debt-to-rent capped below 60% annually
findings.quote: Borrowing of approximately £4,858,565 in 2026/27... The updated Plan now caps the debt to rent position below 60% in any given year. Where the HRA generates a surplus in year this may be used to offset the requirement for additional borrowing which in turn will reduce this number below the 60%. Officers believe this to be a prudent approach and demonstrates fiscal responsibility.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27 Including Rent Setting
findings.headline: The council plans to increase rents by 5% annually from 2027-28 onwards, not the 4% proposed for 2026-27.
findings.detail: Section 4.13 states the Housing Business Plan now assumes a 5% annual rent increase from 2027/28 onwards, across the 35-year lifetime of the plan. This is a material step up from historical RPI+1% or CPI+1% approaches and goes beyond the 4% set for 2026/27. The council acknowledges this 'will be reviewed on an annual basis' and forms part of tenant engagement, but the plan assumes it without additional grant funding or changes to operating model.
findings.matters: A lender funding this council needs to know the financing model assumes 5% rent growth going forward. If tenant satisfaction continues to fall or collection rates slip, the council may face pressure not to deliver those increases, leaving a funding gap in the Business Plan.
findings.figures: 4% increase 2026/27; 5% from 2027/28 onwards across 35-year plan
findings.quote: The Plan now assumes a 5% increase in annual rents is applied across its lifetime from 2027/28 onwards in order to deliver the investment that is deemed necessary to meet legislative targets. However, this is reviewed on an annual basis and forms part of tenant engagement in advance of annual budget setting.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27 Including Rent Setting
findings.headline: Tenant satisfaction with rents has fallen sharply, despite broad support for the 4% increase.
findings.detail: Only 53.78% of tenants now think current rents are fair, down from 68.68% last year. Value-for-money perception has collapsed to 39.08% from 56.56%. The council consulted 238 tenants (6.2% of households) and 86.55% preferred the 4% increase option, but the underlying trend in rent acceptability is declining materially.
findings.matters: Falling tenant satisfaction with rent levels could presage collection difficulties, arrears growth, or neighbourhood tension—all material to council financial stability and lender risk. The council is aware of the divergence between broad support for this specific increase and declining belief that rents are fair.
findings.figures: 53.78% think rents fair (down from 68.68%); 39.08% think value for money (down from 56.56%); 238 responses from 3,840 households (6.2%)
findings.quote: Of those responses the balance of opinion reflected that current rents are fair at 53.78%. However, this is lower than the prior year where 68.68% of tenants deemed the rents to be fair. This reflects the need to continue to meet the demands and challenges of tenants whilst meeting their tenant expectations in relation to fairness.

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND REVENUE MONITORING AS AT PERIOD 8 OF THE 2025/26 FINANCIAL YEAR
findings.headline: Pay bill rising to unachievable levels; future demands unaffordable within funding settlements
findings.detail: The council identifies 'material significance' in the 'potential impact on the Council's pay bill with future demands benchmarked to rising prices setting an unachievable target within existing and planned funding settlements.' This suggests future pay settlements cannot be met from existing budgets and will force further service reductions.
findings.matters: Unaffordable pay costs represent a structural squeeze on the budget that cannot be resolved through service efficiency alone. If pay demands exceed funding, the council faces a deficit even without demand or cost pressures in other areas.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided; flagged as 'material risk' and 'unachievable'
findings.quote: the potential impact on the Council's pay bill with future demands benchmarked to rising prices setting an unachievable target within existing and planned funding settlements.

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND REVENUE MONITORING AS AT PERIOD 8 OF THE 2025/26 FINANCIAL YEAR
findings.headline: Council tax collection rates falling to 73.29%; 97% target 'remains a challenge'
findings.detail: In-year collection rates for November 2025 are 73.29%, a 0.53 percentage point decrease from the prior year. The decline is partly attributable to prior-year cost-of-living credits. findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND REVENUE MONITORING AS AT PERIOD 8 OF THE 2025/26 FINANCIAL YEAR

findings.detail: The council set a £9.425m budget gap for 2025/26, addressed by a 13% council tax increase. The council acknowledged that implementation 'could have a detrimental impact on its communities, businesses and workforce' during the cost-of-living crisis.
findings.matters: A budget strategy that the council itself describes as unsustainable indicates structural unaffordability. A 13% tax rise and the overspend in-year suggests the baseline budget is fundamentally inadequate.

findings.headline: Reserves exhausted and can no longer be relied upon; enhancement required instead of drawdown

Reserves are 'significantly lower than in the prior year' and any future overspends must be 'managed internally.' This marks a shift from historical reliance on reserve drawdowns.

findings.paper_title: GENERAL FUND REVENUE MONITORING AS AT PERIOD 8 OF THE 2025/26 FINANCIAL YEAR

findings.headline: Council maintains under-borrowed position of £32.075m, relying on reserve depletion to fund capital needs rather than borrowing at current rates

findings.matters: The strategy assumes interest rates will fall enough to justify waiting to borrow later. If rates don't fall as forecast, the council will face higher costs and reduced financial flexibility as reserves deplete. findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that HRA debt servicing costs are approaching 40% of net revenue stream, which is unsustainable and leaves little headroom for service pressures or adverse interest rate movements.

findings.headline: Structural budget gap persists; medium-term plan requires "year-on-year difficult decisions" on spending cuts
findings.detail: The council acknowledges a "sustained gap between expenditure and funding requiring, year-on-year, more difficult decisions when the Council sets its Budget". MTFS update due October 2025, continuing to evaluate scenarios across the three-year planning horizon.
findings.matters: A structural gap requiring difficult decisions every year signals the council is cutting to unsustainable levels rather than achieving structural balance—a trajectory that weakens the council's financial foundation and borrowing case.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: this remains challenging within a single year settlement and the sustained gap between expenditure and funding requiring, year-on-year, more difficult decisions when the Council sets its Budget.

findings.paper_title: PR-16-25-GM Revenue Monitoring P3 2025/26
findings.headline: Pay bill inflation poses material risk of exceeding funding settlements
findings.detail: The council identifies "the potential impact on the Council's pay bill with risks that inflation may set an unachievable target within existing and planned funding settlements" as a material risk affecting multiple services and reflecting cost-of-living crisis impacts.
findings.matters: If pay inflation exceeds assumptions embedded in the MTFS, the council will face widening deficits that cannot be resolved by planning or savings, forcing reserve drawdown or emergency service cuts.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this report
findings.quote: Furthermore, and of material significance, is the potential impact on the Council's pay bill with risks that inflation may set an unachievable target within existing and planned funding settlements.

findings.paper_title: PR-16-25-GM Revenue Monitoring P3 2025/26
findings.headline: Education forecasting £1.079m overspend in transport and staffing costs
findings.detail: Education is projected to overspend by £1.079m at Period 3, with the main driver being transport and staffing variations within probationer savings, indicating the council's planned staffing reductions are not being achieved.
findings.matters: Staffing savings are typically the easiest cuts to plan but hardest to deliver; failure to achieve them on a major budget (education) signals difficulty controlling workforce costs and future budget tightness.
findings.figures: £1.079m education overspend
findings.quote: The main area of significance at Period 3 is transport and staffing variations within probationer savings.

findings.paper_title: PR-16-25-GM Revenue Monitoring P3 2025/26
findings.headline: HSCP overspending by £1.046m driven by employee and agency cost pressures
findings.detail: The Health and Social Care Partnership is projecting a year-end overspend of approximately £1.046m at Period 3, with pressures within employee costs (including overtime and other pay) and agency cost expenditure. HSCP budgets represent £83.952m of the council's overall spend.
findings.matters: HSCP overspends threaten the council's overall financial position. Whilst expected to be covered by HSCP reserves, this is a finite fund and the council remains ultimately liable for any shortfall.
findings.figures: £1.046m HSCP overspend, £83.952m HSCP budget
findings.quote: The HSCP is currently projecting a year-end overspend within Social Work budgets of approximately £1.046m at Period 3. These projections are based on how HSCP services are currently being mobilised in accordance with its plan and are expected to be offset, fully or in part, through the use of reserves held by the HSCP.

findings.paper_title: PR-16-25-GM Revenue Monitoring P3 2025/26
findings.headline: General fund reserves significantly depleted with explicit warning of no future headroom
findings.detail: The council states reserves will be "significantly lower than the 2023/24 position" after planned drawdowns, and explicitly warns that "once these reserves have been applied, there will be limited or no capacity to underwrite future budget gaps". Any in-year overspends must now be managed through business critical spend memos.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves remove the council's shock absorber for unexpected costs or demand variations, forcing service cuts or borrowing to cover any further shortfalls and increasing vulnerability to future volatility.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audited reserves position not yet finalised; 2023/24 comparison pending
findings.quote: Once these reserves have been applied, there will be limited or no capacity to underwrite future budget gaps.

findings.paper_title: PR-16-25-GM Revenue Monitoring P3 2025/26
findings.headline: Council forecasting £1.221m overspend requiring reserves drawdown in year one of MTFS
findings.detail: At Period 3, the council is projecting a general fund revenue overspend of £1.221m (excluding HSCP), which will require drawdown of general fund reserves. This follows a £9.425m budget gap in 2025/26 that was closed by a 13% council tax increase.
findings.matters: In-year overspends requiring reserve drawdown signal that the council's budget assumptions are not holding and reserves are being depleted faster than planned, reducing financial flexibility for future years.
findings.figures: £1.221m overspend, 13% council tax increase, £9.425m budget gap
findings.quote: A Council overspend of £1.221m equates to an in-year gap and potential drawdown of General Fund reserves equating to £1.221m, as there was no gap in budget due to the increase in Council Tax as set out above.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Housing Capital Monitoring Report Period 3 25-26
findings.headline: £2.4m Glasgow Road affordable housing development carried forward despite explicitly uncertain viability
findings.detail: The Glasgow Road, Kirkintilloch site (planned for 54 units, £2.406m allocation) is noted as having unresolved viability questions. The document states it is 'provisionally included subject to refinement of access / junction design', yet the scheme remains in the capital plan at full budget with projected year-end spend of £2.406m matching the budget allocation. No variance is shown despite the viability uncertainty.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether material capital schemes are firm commitments or provisional carries subject to design/viability resolution, as failure to proceed would reduce affordable housing supply and affect capital programme delivery and actual borrowing requirements
findings.figures: £2.406m allocated and projected; 54 units; forms part of £15.376m new-build programme 2025-2030
findings.quote: development viabiltiy remains uncertain, provisionally included subject to refinement of access / junction design
